Other recurring principles include precaution (Rio Principle 15), under which lack of full scientific certainty should not postpone cost-effective measures to prevent serious or irreversible damage; the polluter pays principle (Principle 16); sustainable development; common but differentiated responsibilities, recognising that states have different capacities and historic contributions; and cooperation and the duty to notify and consult. Whether precaution is a binding customary rule or a general approach is debated, and tribunals have treated it cautiously.

Treaties address specific problems. The Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer 1985 and its Montreal Protocol of 1987 phase out ozone-depleting substances through binding schedules, with trade measures to encourage participation and a fund to help developing countries; it is often described as one of the most successful environmental agreements. The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change 1992 set the overall framework for climate cooperation, the Kyoto Protocol 1997 set binding targets for developed countries, and the Paris Agreement 2015, in force since 2016, takes a different approach. It aims to hold the increase in global average temperature to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees, and it relies on nationally determined contributions, which each party prepares and communicates, with transparency and periodic review (the global stocktake), rather than on binding national targets. States' obligations to submit and pursue contributions are binding in a procedural sense, while the level of ambition is largely left to the states themselves. Other important agreements concern biodiversity, the trade in endangered species (CITES 1973), hazardous wastes (the Basel Convention 1989) and marine pollution.

International courts have been asked about climate obligations. As of this writing, the ICJ has delivered an advisory opinion in 2025 on the obligations of states in respect of climate change, following a request by the General Assembly; this is a fast-moving area and learners should consult the opinion itself and current developments.

Worked example: State A operates a chemical plant near its border, and emissions harm crops in State B. Under the prevention principle, A must exercise due diligence to prevent significant transboundary harm, which includes conducting an impact assessment and notifying and consulting B before approving risky activity. B can claim responsibility under state responsibility rules once significant harm is shown, even though A's plant is lawful under A's own law.

lessons.title: Space Law: The Outer Space Treaty Regime
body: Space law grew out of the early years of space flight, when states were anxious to prevent the competition between the Soviet Union and the United States from extending conflict and claims into space. Its core is the Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies of 1967, usually called the Outer Space Treaty, which has a very large number of parties, including all major space powers. Many of its principles are regarded as customary.

The main rules are as follows. Article I provides that exploration and use of outer space shall be carried out for the benefit and in the interests of all countries and is the province of all mankind; outer space is free for exploration and use by all states without discrimination, on a basis of equality. Article II provides that outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means. This is the non-appropriation principle, and it means no state can lawfully claim sovereignty over the Moon or a planet. Article III applies international law, including the UN Charter, to space activities. Article IV prohibits placing in orbit around the Earth, installing on celestial bodies or stationing in space any nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction, and requires that the Moon and other celestial bodies be used exclusively for peaceful purposes, with military bases and testing of weapons of any kind banned on celestial bodies. The treaty does not ban all military uses of space: conventional military satellites and ballistic missiles that transit space are not prohibited by it. Article VI is a key innovation: states bear international responsibility for national activities in outer space, whether carried on by governmental agencies or by non-governmental

entities, and the activities of private entities require authorisation and continuing supervision by the appropriate state. This is why a state licences its commercial launch companies. Article VII provides that a state that launches or procures the launching of an object, or from whose territory it is launched, is internationally liable for damage caused by the object. Article VIII retains jurisdiction and control of a registered space object, and ownership of objects is not affected by being in space. Article IX requires due regard to the interests of other states, avoiding harmful contamination, and consultation before potentially harmful activity.

Further treaties build on this. The Rescue Agreement 1968 requires assistance to astronauts and return of astronauts and space objects. The Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects 1972 (the Liability Convention) makes a launching state absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the Earth or to aircraft in flight (Article II), and liable on the basis of fault for damage caused elsewhere, for example in orbit (Article III). The first major claim was after the Soviet satellite Cosmos 954, carrying a nuclear reactor, scattered radioactive debris over Canada in 1978; Canada claimed compensation and the matter was settled by a protocol in 1981 for a sum lower than Canada's claim. The Registration Convention 1975 requires states to register space objects. The Moon Agreement 1979 declares the Moon and its resources to be the common heritage of mankind, but has few parties and none of the major space powers.

Commercial activity raises current questions. The Outer Space Treaty bans national appropriation of celestial bodies, but it does not say clearly whether private extraction of resources, such as mining of asteroids or lunar material, is permitted. The United States passed a law in 2015 recognising the right of its citizens to own resources they extract, and several states have passed similar laws. Many states take the view that extraction of resources is consistent with the treaty as long as no sovereignty is claimed, while others argue that national authorisation of ownership comes close to appropriation. The Artemis Accords of 2020, a set of non-binding political principles led by the United States, support resource extraction and "safety zones" around activities; their legal status and the question of safety zones are debated. Space debris, congestion and the limited availability of orbital slots and radio spectrum, managed by the International Telecommunication Union, also raise growing legal issues.

Worked example: A privately owned company in State A launches a satellite that collides in orbit with a satellite of State B. Under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, A is responsible for the company's activity, and under Article III of the Liability Convention, A is liable to B only if the damage is due to the fault of A or persons for whom A is responsible, because the damage occurred in orbit. If the satellite had instead fallen on a village on Earth, A would be absolutely liable regardless of fault.

questions.prompt: Which description best captures how international law is made and applied compared with domestic law?
choices: Its main lawmakers are the states bound by it, acting through treaties and custom
A world parliament enacts binding statutes that a global police force then enforces against each member state
It is made only by a supreme international court whose rulings automatically become binding law for every state
It is made by the Security Council alone, which adopts general rules binding all states by majority vote

questions.prompt: Article 2(1) of the UN Charter states sovereign equality. What does that principle mean in law?
choices: Great powers hold greater legal rights because their capacity to enforce rules is greater
States have equal legal status whatever their size or power
States must hold equal voting shares in every international organisation to which they belong
Small states are exempt from rules that bind larger states, so as to compensate for weakness

questions.prompt: A UN mediator is killed while on duty and the UN wants to bring a claim against the responsible state. In the Reparation for Injuries opinion (ICJ, 1949), what did the Court conclude about the UN?
choices: It has the same full range of sovereign powers as a state, including territorial jurisdiction over its offices
It has personality only toward states that expressly recognised it when they joined the organisation
It has international legal personality and the capacity to bring such claims
It has no personality of its own and only member states may present claims on behalf of their own nationals

questions.prompt: State A has not ratified a multilateral treaty banning a certain weapon. State B, a party, says A is nonetheless bound because "the treaty binds the whole international community". Which response is most accurate?
choices: A is bound, since a treaty adopted by a majority of states becomes binding on every state after a reasonable period
A is not bound under any circumstances, because a treaty can never be the source of a customary rule
A is bound if the weapon is dangerous enough, because danger of a weapon automatically creates a peremptory norm
A is bound only if the ban also exists as a customary rule or A has otherwise consented

questions.prompt: State Q's government argues that international law is "not real law" because no authority compels it to obey. State Q then publishes a legal memorandum defending its border operation as consistent with the UN Charter. What is the best analytic point to make about this?
choices: Q's effort to justify its conduct in legal terms indicates that it treats international rules as binding
The memorandum proves that the border operation was lawful, since a state's own legal opinion is conclusive
The memorandum is legally irrelevant because only decisions of the International Court of Justice can state the law
The memorandum shows that international law is merely a branch of Q's domestic law and depends on Q's own approval

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the sources listed in Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute as something the Court applies?
choices: International conventions establishing rules recognised by the contesting states
International custom as evidence of a general practice accepted as law
General principles of law recognised by civilised nations
Resolutions of the Security Council adopted by a simple majority as general legislation

questions.prompt: Under Article 59 of the ICJ Statute, what is the legal force of an ICJ decision?
choices: It binds only the losing party and has no effect for the winning party
It binds the parties and also every state that is a member of the United Nations
It binds only the parties and only for that particular case
It binds all states as precedent, as a common-law appellate decision binds lower courts

questions.prompt: In the Temple of Preah Vihear case (ICJ, 1962), the Court relied on Thailand's long acceptance of a map without objection. Which type of source does this reasoning illustrate?
choices: A subsidiary means consisting of the writings of leading publicists on frontier maps
General principles such as acquiescence and estoppel based on fairness and consistency
A multilateral convention binding Thailand through its ratification of the treaty
A peremptory norm overriding the consent of Thailand to a different frontier

questions.prompt: State R owes State S obligations under a bilateral trade treaty. The UN Security Council later adopts a binding Chapter VII sanctions decision requiring R to stop all trade with S. R's obligations under the two instruments conflict. Which rule most directly resolves the conflict?
choices: Article 103 of the UN Charter, under which Charter obligations prevail over conflicting obligations under other agreements
Article 59 of the ICJ Statute, under which the later instrument binds only the parties to the earlier one
The general rule that the older treaty prevails because it is the more specific and settled commitment
Article 38(2) of the ICJ Statute, which allows R to choose whichever instrument is fairer to it

questions.prompt: A General Assembly resolution on a principle of non-intervention was adopted by consensus and has been repeatedly cited by states as stating the law. An advocate says it is a binding statute. A better analysis is that the resolution:
choices: Is binding because the General Assembly has general legislative power over all member states
Is legally meaningless because states cannot create law by votes in international organisations
Is a peremptory norm because it was adopted by consensus rather than by a majority
Is not binding in itself but may be evidence of opinio juris contributing to customary law

questions.prompt: Which two elements are needed to form a rule of customary international law?
choices: A resolution of the Security Council and approval by the International Court of Justice
Repeated use for at least fifty years and a general vote of the General Assembly
State practice and opinio juris, meaning a belief that the conduct is legally required or permitted
A written agreement and ratification by two thirds of the states in the world

questions.prompt: In North Sea Continental Shelf (ICJ, 1969), why was Germany not bound by the equidistance rule in Article 6 of the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf?
choices: Germany had made a reservation to Article 6 that the Court treated as valid and effective
The convention had been terminated by the later practice of the Netherlands and Denmark
The Court held that treaty rules can never generate custom binding non-parties
Germany had not ratified the convention

questions.prompt: A state objects openly and consistently from the earliest stages to an emerging customary rule on baselines. If the rule later crystallises, what is the likely result under the persistent objector doctrine?
choices: The rule will not be opposable to that state, unless the rule is a peremptory norm
The rule binds that state, since custom binds all states regardless of any objection
The rule binds that state only after it has obtained approval from the Security Council
The rule is void, since a single objection prevents any custom from forming

questions.prompt: For three decades most coastal states have inspected cargo vessels at a particular distance from shore, citing "customary rights". State T did the same, but its foreign ministry states that it does so solely as a courtesy to neighbours and without any legal obligation. State U, a neighbour, claims a customary rule exists binding T. What is the strongest analysis?
choices: No rule can exist because custom requires practice by all states without exception
T's statements negate opinio juris on its side, so U must show that opinio juris exists among states generally
The rule exists conclusively because practice has lasted three decades, and T's statements are legally irrelevant
The rule exists because any practice that many states follow automatically becomes custom after thirty years

questions.prompt: State V enters a treaty with State W in which the two agree that either may use force against nationals of the other for any reason. A third state argues that the treaty is void on a ground drawn from the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969. Which provision best supports this?
choices: Article 31, which makes treaties void if their wording departs from ordinary meaning
Article 62, which makes treaties void whenever one party regrets the bargain it struck
Article 53, which makes a treaty void if it conflicts with a peremptory norm of general international law
Article 26, which makes treaties void if they are not ratified by every state in the world

questions.prompt: Which of the following is one of the Montevideo Convention (1933) criteria for statehood?
choices: Recognition by all permanent members of the Security Council
A permanent population
A democratic constitution
Membership of the United Nations

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the declaratory theory of recognition from the constitutive theory?
choices: Under the declaratory theory statehood exists once the criteria are met and recognition merely acknowledges it
Under the declaratory theory a state exists only for those states that have formally recognised it
Under the constitutive theory statehood arises automatically and recognition has no political consequence
Under the constitutive theory a state is created only by a vote of the UN General Assembly

questions.prompt: What did the ICJ conclude in its 2010 advisory opinion on Kosovo's declaration of independence?
choices: That Kosovo had become a state with a right to remedial secession under international law
That the declaration was void because only the Security Council can create new states
That the declaration was unlawful because it breached the territorial integrity of Serbia
That the declaration did not violate general international law

questions.prompt: Province Z has a population of 2 million, clear borders and a capable government, and declares independence from State Y after Y's army is ordered into the province. Y was not oppressing the province, and no armed conflict preceded the declaration. Three states recognise Z. A lawyer for Z says that statehood is now complete. The strongest response is:
choices: Z cannot be a state because states cannot be created from the territory of an existing state under any circumstances
Z becomes a state automatically on the day after the declaration because international law provides for it

Recognition by three states does not establish statehood by itself; Z's claim must meet the Montevideo criteria and the rules on the lawful creation of states, and there is no general right to secession outside colonial contexts
Statehood is complete because three recognitions satisfy the constitutive theory, which counts only a minimum of recognising states

questions.prompt: After a coup, the military of State K removes the elected government and takes control of the capital. The new regime announces it will not honour K's existing treaty debts. A creditor state argues that K remains bound. Which analysis is most accurate?
choices: K is bound only if the creditor state recognises the new regime, which is a condition of statehood
The state's identity and treaty obligations continue despite the change of government
K's treaty obligations are extinguished because the former government no longer exists
K ceases to be a state until the new regime is recognised by the Security Council

questions.prompt: Which term describes a state's authority to carry out law through arrests, seizures and similar acts?
choices: Enforcement jurisdiction
Prescriptive jurisdiction
Adjudicative jurisdiction
Protective jurisdiction

questions.prompt: State D forges the passports of State E in order to pass off its agents abroad. Which basis of jurisdiction most directly supports prosecution in State E of the forgers when they are later found within E?
choices: The universality principle, which applies only to crimes such as piracy and genocide
The protective principle, which covers conduct abroad that threatens the security or essential functions of the state
The passive personality principle, which depends on the victim being a national
The nationality principle, which depends on the offender being a national of the state

questions.prompt: What approach to jurisdiction did the PCIJ adopt in the Lotus case (1927)?
choices: A state may exercise jurisdiction only over conduct taking place within its own territory
A state may exercise jurisdiction only where the offender is present within the national territory
A state may exercise jurisdiction over foreign conduct unless a prohibitive rule of international law forbids it
A state may exercise jurisdiction only where a permissive rule of international law expressly grants it

questions.prompt: A national of State P assaults a national of State R in the territory of State Q. Later, the assailant travels to State R. Officers of State R, acting without Q's consent, arrest the assailant while he is visiting State Q's capital and take him to R for trial. What is the strongest analysis of R's conduct?
choices: The arrest was lawful because R's passive personality jurisdiction covers any step needed to bring the assailant to trial
The arrest was lawful because the assailant is a national of P and P has jurisdiction, which R may exercise on P's behalf
The arrest was lawful because enforcement jurisdiction follows the victim's nationality in all states
The arrest violated Q's territorial sovereignty because enforcement jurisdiction cannot be exercised on foreign soil without consent, even if R had a basis for prescribing law

questions.prompt: Two vessels, one flying the flag of State F and one carrying the flag of State G, collide on the high seas, killing a crew member on the G vessel. State G prosecutes the F captain once the vessel enters a G port. Under Article 97 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea 1982, which analysis is most accurate?
choices: G may not prosecute: only the flag state or the state of nationality of the person concerned may bring penal proceedings in respect of a collision at sea
G may prosecute freely: the Lotus decision still allows any state affected by a collision to take proceedings
G may prosecute only if it first obtains a resolution authorising it from the UN General Assembly
G may prosecute because the ship entered its port, and port presence overrides the rule about collisions

questions.prompt: Under Article 2(1)(a) of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, which feature is essential for an instrument to be a treaty?
choices: It must be approved by the UN General Assembly before it can create binding obligations
It must be signed by every state that will later be affected by its provisions
It must be named a treaty or convention, since the title decides its legal status
It must be an international agreement between states in written form and governed by international law

questions.prompt: A state signs a treaty that requires ratification but has not yet ratified it. Under Article 18 of the VCLT, what is its position?
choices: It is fully bound by every obligation in the treaty from the moment of signature
It is free to do anything, since signature creates no legal consequence of any kind
It must refrain from acts that would defeat the object and purpose of the treaty until it makes its intention clear
It must ratify within twelve months or lose all rights it could have claimed under the treaty

questions.prompt: What did the ICJ hold in the Reservations to the Genocide Convention advisory opinion (1951)?
choices: A state may not become a party if any other party objects to its reservation
A reserving state remains a party only if the reservation is compatible with the object and purpose of the convention
Reservations to multilateral treaties are never permitted unless every party accepts them in advance
Reservations are valid whatever their content so long as the reserving state ratifies the treaty

questions.prompt: State A ratifies a multilateral human rights treaty with a reservation excluding "any obligation that conflicts with A's domestic law, as it may exist from time to time." State B objects, stating the reservation defeats the treaty's object and purpose, but does not say it opposes the treaty entering into force between itself and A. Which analysis is most defensible?
choices: The reservation is likely impermissible under Article 19(c) because it is vague and subordinates the treaty to national law
The reservation is valid because Article 19 allows any reservation unless the treaty itself prohibits reservations expressly
The treaty cannot enter into force between A and B at all, because any objection to a reservation prevents entry into force
The reservation is valid because B's objection was not made through the Security Council, which is the only competent organ

questions.prompt: The foreign minister of State C signs a boundary agreement with State D, without producing full powers. C's president later says the minister had no authority and that C is not bound. Which response best reflects the VCLT?
choices: C is not bound, because only a head of state may sign a treaty and a minister cannot do so
C is not bound, because every signature must be accompanied by written full powers presented to the other party
The agreement is binding only once the Security Council has confirmed the minister's authority
A foreign minister is considered to represent the state for treaty-making acts under Article 7 without needing full powers, so C is likely bound if consent was otherwise expressed

questions.prompt: Which rule does Article 26 of the VCLT state?
choices: A state may refuse performance whenever its internal law prohibits compliance
Treaties lapse automatically after twenty years unless the parties renew them
Every treaty in force binds its parties and must be performed by them in good faith
A treaty binds parties only when a majority of states has ratified it

questions.prompt: Under the general rule of interpretation in Article 31 of the VCLT, which element comes first in the analysis?
choices: The subjective intention of the state with the greatest bargaining power during the negotiations
The interpretation adopted by whichever state first performed the obligation under the treaty
The preparatory work and circumstances of conclusion, which the Convention treats as the primary evidence of intent
The ordinary meaning of the terms in their context and in the light of the treaty's object and purpose

questions.prompt: State A and State B conclude a treaty. State C is not a party and has not consented to it. What is the effect of the treaty on C under Article 34?
choices: It creates no obligation or right for C without C's consent
It creates an obligation for C if the treaty says the parties intend it to bind others
It creates an obligation for C if C benefits indirectly from the arrangement
It creates an obligation for C once a majority of the states in the region have ratified it

questions.prompt: A treaty between State E and State F obliges both to give "vehicles" free transit over a shared bridge. E bans motorbikes at the bridge, saying the treaty covers only cars and trucks, and cites a negotiating draft that listed "motor vehicles" which was later changed to "vehicles". F says motorbikes are included. Which approach would a tribunal apply?
choices: Decide in favour of F, because every ambiguity in a treaty is resolved against the party that drafted the text
Begin with the ordinary meaning of "vehicles" in context and in light of the treaty's purpose
Begin with the negotiating draft, which prevails over the final text whenever the two differ in wording
Decide in favour of E, because restrictions on sovereignty must always be read narrowly against the state invoking them

questions.prompt: Hungary in the Gabcikovo-Nagymaros dispute (ICJ, 1997) suspended and then abandoned works, relying on necessity, and purported to terminate the 1977 treaty. Which conclusion did the Court reach?
choices: Hungary was entitled to terminate because ecological risks always override treaty obligations
The treaty had lapsed through the dissolution of Czechoslovakia, which ended all obligations
Hungary's termination was not lawful and the treaty remained in force
The treaty was void from the start because it conflicted with a peremptory norm protecting the environment

questions.prompt: Under Article 53 of the VCLT, what is the consequence of a treaty conflicting with a peremptory norm at the time of its conclusion?
choices: The treaty is valid but must be interpreted narrowly to avoid the conflict
The treaty is void
The treaty is suspended until the next session of the General Assembly
The treaty is voidable at the option of the weaker party only

questions.prompt: A state wishes to withdraw from a treaty that has no termination or denunciation clause. Under Article 56, when may it withdraw?
choices: Only if it is established that the parties intended to admit denunciation or it is implied by the nature of the treaty, with twelve months' notice
Only if the UN Security Council approves the withdrawal by a vote of nine members
Only if a majority of the other parties vote to permit it after a period of five years
Whenever it chooses, since sovereignty allows any state to leave any treaty at will

questions.prompt: Why can the fundamental change of circumstances doctrine in Article 62 not be used by a state seeking to escape a boundary treaty?
choices: Boundary treaties are peremptory norms and therefore can never be affected by any change
Boundary treaties are governed by customary law only and so fall outside the VCLT
Article 62 applies only to treaties of commerce and not to any territorial arrangement
Article 62(2) excludes treaties establishing a boundary from the doctrine

questions.prompt: Under duress from an invasion threat, State A signs a treaty in which it cedes a coastal strip to State B. B had mobilised troops on the border and told A's government it would attack the capital unless the treaty was signed. Years later A says the treaty is void. What is the best analysis?
choices: The treaty is void only if A obtains a ruling from the Security Council that B committed aggression
The treaty is valid because the signing was done by A's authorised representative
The treaty is void under Article 52 if the threat was a threat of force in violation of the principles of the UN Charter
The treaty is valid unless A can show that B's economic pressure was the true cause of A's consent

questions.prompt: State P and State Q are parties to a bilateral treaty of friendship and trade. P materially breaches by repudiating the treaty without legal basis. Q wants to respond. What does Article 60 of the VCLT permit?
choices: Q may terminate the treaty only if P first consents in writing to the termination of its own obligations
Q may terminate the treaty or suspend its operation in whole or in part
Q must continue to perform the treaty in full, because breach by one party can never justify any response by another
Q may terminate the treaty only after a judgment of the ICJ confirms that P has committed a material breach

questions.prompt: What does Article 27 of the VCLT provide about a state's internal law?
choices: A party may not invoke its internal law as justification for failure to perform a treaty
A party may invoke its internal law only where the other parties have approved it
A party may invoke its internal law to justify its failure to perform a treaty
A party may rely on its internal law only when its constitution is more recent than the treaty

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a dualist from a monist approach to international law?
choices: Dualism treats treaties as automatically part of national law, while monism requires legislation
Dualism treats international and national law as separate systems so that treaties generally require legislation before domestic courts apply them
Dualism applies only to customary rules while monism applies only to treaties
Dualism is used only by common law states and monism only by states with written constitutions

questions.prompt: In Medellin v. Texas (U.S., 2008), what did the Supreme Court hold concerning the ICJ's Avena judgment?
choices: The judgment was void because the ICJ lacks authority to decide cases involving the United States
The judgment bound only the federal courts and did not affect state criminal proceedings at all
The judgment was not directly enforceable as domestic law in state court
The judgment was directly enforceable in state courts as federal law because it is a treaty obligation

questions.prompt: The United States ratifies a treaty with the Senate's consent, and the treaty states that parties will "provide" a private right of action but Congress passes no implementing legislation. A litigant sues a state official under the treaty, and the state argues the treaty is non-self-executing. Which analysis is most accurate?
choices: The litigant wins automatically because every treaty is directly enforceable under the Supremacy Clause
The litigant loses and the United States is not in breach, since domestic law decides international responsibility
The treaty is void because Congress did not pass a statute within a reasonable period after ratification
If the treaty is non-self-executing the courts will generally not apply it directly

questions.prompt: Congress passes a statute inconsistent with an earlier ratified treaty to which the United States is a party. In a domestic case between private parties, which answer best states the usual consequence?
choices: The later statute generally prevails domestically under the last-in-time rule
The courts must refer the question to the International Court of Justice before deciding
The treaty prevails because treaties always outrank federal statutes under Article VI
The statute is void because Congress has no authority to legislate contrary to a treaty

questions.prompt: According to Article 2 of the ILC Articles on State Responsibility (2001), what are the two elements of an internationally wrongful act?
choices: A decision of an international court, and a refusal by the state concerned to comply with that decision
A violation of the state's own constitution, and a resulting loss suffered by the state's own citizens
Conduct attributable to the state under international law
Physical injury to a foreign national, and a formal protest lodged by the injured state's government

questions.prompt: A provincial police unit of a federal state beats a detained foreign national in breach of an international obligation, and the federal government says it has no control over provincial police. What is the position under Article 4 of the Articles?
choices: The conduct is attributable only if the federal government approved the unit's conduct in advance and in writing
The conduct is attributable to the province alone, and the injured state must sue the province in its own courts
The conduct is not attributable to the federal state because provincial authorities are separate legal entities in domestic law
The conduct is attributable to the state as the act of a state organ, whatever the organ's position in the state's structure

questions.prompt: In the Corfu Channel case (ICJ, 1949), on what ground did the Court hold Albania responsible for damage to British warships from mines?
choices: Albania knew or must have known of the mines in its waters and failed to warn the ships
Albania had refused to allow the warships to pass through the strait under any circumstances
Albania's agents had laid the mines, which the evidence proved directly during the proceedings
Albania had approved the earlier laying of the mines by a third state in a secret treaty

questions.prompt: State N supplies arms and funding to an armed group in State M and gives general strategic advice, but the group chooses its own targets and operates independently. The group commits a massacre in M. Under the effective control test applied by the ICJ in the Nicaragua and Bosnian Genocide cases, what is the most likely result?
choices: The massacre is attributable to N because N financed and armed the group as a whole
The massacre is not attributable to N unless N directed or effectively controlled the specific operation
The massacre is attributable to M, because the group is a state organ of the territory in which it operates
The massacre is attributable to N only if a Security Council resolution has condemned the group's leaders

questions.prompt: Paramilitaries not controlled by State S commit genocide in a neighbouring region. S had strong influence over them, knew of the serious risk and had the capacity to act, but did nothing. Using the reasoning of the ICJ in Bosnia v. Serbia (2007), what is the best analysis of S's responsibility?
choices: S bears no responsibility of any kind, because the acts of private groups can never give rise to state responsibility
S is responsible only if the paramilitaries were formally part of its armed forces under its domestic law
S may be responsible for breaching its separate obligation to prevent genocide
S is responsible for committing genocide, since influence is the equivalent of control for attribution

questions.prompt: Under the ILC Articles, which of the following is a form of reparation listed in Article 34?
choices: Retorsion
Retaliation
Sanction
